cited_details.statement: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a model compression and knowledge transfer mechanism in which a large teacher model transfers learned behavior to a smaller student model [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].

The motivation behind the technique stems from the fact that modern deep learning models often achieve state-of-the-art performance at the cost of massive computational resources, making them impractical for real-time or edge deployment [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].

KD addresses this tension by transferring the capabilities of large models into smaller, efficient ones without significant loss in accuracy, producing a model that is faster, lighter, and suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices such as mobile phones or embedded systems [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].
The goal is typically to have the student model's accuracy approach, or sometimes even exceed, the teacher's accuracy [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].

in "Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network," which demonstrated that an ensemble of large models can be compressed into a single smaller, more deployable model [https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531].

The abstract notes that a very simple way to improve the performance of almost any machine learning algorithm is to train many different models on the same data and then average their predictions, but that making predictions using a whole ensemble is cumbersome and may be too computationally expensive to allow deployment to a large number of users [https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531].

The work builds on earlier work by Caruana and collaborators showing that it is possible to compress the knowledge in an ensemble into a single model, and develops this approach further using a different compression technique, achieving surprising results on MNIST and significantly improving a heavily used commercial acoustic model [https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531].

abstract also introduces a new type of ensemble composed of one or more full models and many specialist models which learn to distinguish fine-grained classes that the full models confuse, and notes that unlike a mixture of experts, these specialist models can be trained rapidly and in parallel [https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531].
(2015), stating that a compact model can be trained to reproduce the behavior and performance of a more complex model [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].

The teacher-student framework involves first training a complex teacher network, such as a deep neural network with many parameters, on the target task [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].

For each example in the training set, the input is then passed through the teacher to obtain its output probabilities, which become the soft targets or teacher's probability distribution over classes [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].

The student network is trained on the same task, but instead of learning only from ground-truth labels, it learns to match the teacher model's predictions, the soft probabilities over classes [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].

A distillation loss, often implemented as the Kullback–Leibler divergence between teacher and student outputs, is combined with a standard supervised loss to align the student's outputs with the teacher's [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].
(2015), softens the teacher's probability distribution to provide richer supervisory signal than hard labels alone [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].

Originally applied in computer vision for tasks such as image classification and recognition, and later in natural language processing, KD is now common whenever large and complex models need to be compressed [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].
Response-based knowledge refers to distilling the final outputs of the teacher, often the soft probability distribution across all classes [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].
Feature-based knowledge, by contrast, leverages intermediate representations from the teacher's hidden layers [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].

explicitly proposed using hints from intermediate layers to address the network compression problem by taking advantage of depth, with the goal of training thin and deep student networks [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1412.6550].

Relation-based knowledge forms a third category, capturing relationships between different examples or feature maps rather than individual outputs [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].

In the standard offline setting, the teacher is pre-trained and fixed, while in online distillation, the teacher and student are co-trained rather than treated as a static authority [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].

Multi-teacher distillation extends the framework to use multiple teachers simultaneously, with use cases including leveraging an ensemble of models as a single compact model [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].
Self-distillation is another recognized variant, in which the model teaches itself, often via its own layers [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].

KD has also been applied across different data modalities, with cross-modal distillation referring to settings where teacher and student operate on different modalities [https://www.lightly.ai/blog/knowledge-distillation].
